# Yardhand

> A self-hosted gateway: one endpoint for every tool behind it, from MCP servers and REST APIs its owner connected.
> Find a tool by what you want to do, read its input schema, run it. Over MCP at `/mcp`, or over REST here.
> Send `Authorization: Bearer <key>` on every call (one key per client), or an OAuth token the owner approves.

## Start

- MCP clients: connect to `/mcp`. You get `search_tools`, `describe_tool`, `call_tool`, `get_result`,
  `list_upstreams`, `read_resource`, `get_playbook`, and any tools pinned for your key. The server instructions list
  the upstreams you may use, and mark those with a manual. Playbooks are also listed as prompts (slash commands).
- REST clients: `GET /api` links to everything. The usual path is three calls:
  1. `GET /api/tools?q=<what you want to do>`: tools across every upstream, best match first.
  2. `GET /api/tools/{name}`: the tool's description and JSON Schema input.
  3. `POST /api/calls` with `{"tool": "<name>", "arguments": {…}}`, or `POST /api/tools/{name}/calls` with the
     arguments as the whole body. The answer carries the tool's own result (`result.content`, and
     `result.structuredContent` when it declares an output schema).
- Typed clients: `GET /api/tools/openapi.json` describes every tool your key may use as an OpenAPI 3.1 operation.
- The owner manages the gateway in the browser at `/app` (connections, keys, reviews, the call log). Everything there
  is an `/api` route too, but those routes answer only the owner's key: a client key gets 403.

## Manuals, playbooks and links

Some upstreams say more than their tools do:

- A **manual**: how the upstream wants its tools used. Read it once before its tools: `read_resource`
  `gateway://u/<upstream>/manual` (MCP), or `GET /api/manuals/{name}`. `GET /api/manuals` lists them; MCP clients with
  the Skills extension also get them as skills (`skill://<manual>/SKILL.md`). The gateway adds a short note at the
  top saying how its tools and links are named here; the rest is as the upstream wrote it.
- **Playbooks**: the upstream's step-by-step way to do one task (its MCP prompts). `search_tools` (and
  `GET /api/tools?q=…`, in `playbooks`) suggests one when it fits; `get_playbook` or
  `GET /api/playbooks/{name}/messages?arguments={…}` fills it in. Named `<upstream>-<prompt>`.
- **Links** a tool returns, like `cookbook://recipes/123`: read them as they came with `read_resource` or
  `GET /api/resources?uri=…`; the gateway finds the upstream by the scheme. `GET /api/links` lists the kinds.

Reading any of these uses the upstream's credential and is logged like a call, but needs no write scope.

## Pack keys

A key can be locked to a **pack**: a kit for one kind of work, curated by the owner. `GET /api/me` says so
(`pack`). A pack key sees only the pack: its tools are listed directly over MCP (in the pack's own wording), its
description is the server instructions, and search, `describe_tool`, playbooks, manuals and calls stay inside it. A
call to anything else is refused (403) and logged; the per-upstream passthrough (`/u/{id}/mcp`) is refused too. A
pack key opens only the links its tools returned in the last day (through `/u/{upstream}/r/…` and `read_resource`).
Keys can expire: a 403 says when.

## Rules worth knowing

- Tool names are `<upstream>.<tool>`, e.g. `cookbook.research_recipes`.
- A tool that changes things (`needsWrite: true`, `[changes things]` in MCP) needs a key with write scope; a
  read-only key never sees those tools.
- The owner can switch tools off: one tool, a group of a connection's tools, or everything on a connection that
  changes or deletes things. An off tool is left out of lists and searches; calling it anyway is a 403 whose `detail`
  says which switch is off. Ask the owner rather than looking for another way round.
- Over MCP, a result bigger than your key's cap is cut: you get page 1 and a call id; `get_result` (or
  `GET /api/calls/{id}/result?page=2`) gives the rest for an hour. REST answers are never cut.
- `POST` runs accept `Idempotency-Key`: a retried request with the same key answers the first result again.
- Calls are rate-limited per key (`RateLimit` headers; 429 with `Retry-After` when over).
- Errors are `application/problem+json` with a `detail` that says what to do next: arguments that don't match
  the tool's input schema are a 400 listing each bad field in `errors`, before the upstream is called. A tool
  that ran and reported its own failure answers 200 with `status: "tool_error"` and `result.isError: true`.
- Links in a result that point at an upstream's own host are rewritten to `/u/{upstream}/r/<path>`: open them
  with the same key (read-only, through the gateway).
- A connection's tools come in groups (`groups` on `GET /api/upstreams`, printed by `list_upstreams`): narrow a
  search to one with `group` and `upstream` (`search_tools`, or `GET /api/tools?upstream=…&group=…`).
- In lists a tool has a short `summary`; `GET /api/tools/{name}` gives the full `description` and schemas.
- Lists are HAL: follow `_links.next` until it is absent.
- Send W3C trace context (a `traceparent` header on REST, `_meta.traceparent` on MCP) and each call is recorded as a
  span inside your own trace; without it, each call is a trace of its own. Only metadata is traced, never arguments
  or results.
